prompt: Let $A$ be a set and $R\subseteq A\times A$ a binary relation on $A$. For $x,y\in A$, write $R(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in R$. Which condition defines connexity on distinct elements? Here connexity only compares distinct elements.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\; (x\ne y\Rightarrow (R(x,y)\lor R(y,x)))$.
answers.explanation: Every pair of distinct elements is comparable in at least one direction. This convention imposes no condition on loops.
Every related pair has its reverse; loops are allowed but not required. This defines symmetry, not connexity on distinct elements.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(y,x))\Rightarrow x=y)$.
answers.explanation: Mutual relatedness forces equality. Self-loops are allowed. This defines antisymmetry, not connexity on distinct elements.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\;\forall z\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(y,z))\Rightarrow R(x,z))$.
answers.explanation: Every two-step chain has its direct shortcut, including chains with repeated vertices. This defines transitivity, not connexity on distinct elements.
Each element has at least one outgoing related element, which may be itself. This defines seriality, not connexity on distinct elements.
Every ordered pair is present, including every loop. This defines universality, not connexity on distinct elements.
Every related pair has no reverse. Taking the two elements equal also forbids loops. This defines asymmetry, not connexity on distinct elements.
Every pair is comparable, including an element with itself, so all loops are required. This defines comparability including equal elements, not connexity on distinct elements.

answers.text: $\forall x\in A\;\forall y\in A\;\forall z\in A\; ((R(x,y)\land R(x,z))\Rightarrow y=z)$.
answers.explanation: An element has at most one outgoing related element; it need not have any. This defines right-uniqueness, not connexity on distinct elements.
One related pair suffices; the other elements may be isolated. This defines nonemptiness, not connexity on distinct elements.
